messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rami's Story

Rami Khalil was forty-two when two off-duty police officers assaulted him in the parking garage of his apartment building in Arlington. He had been leaving for work early on a Tuesday morning, carrying his laptop bag, when they approached him from behind a concrete pillar. What began as aggressive questioning about his presence in the building—he lived there, had lived there for six years—escalated into a physical and sexual assault that lasted perhaps eight minutes but fractured something irretrievable in how he understood his body and the world around him. One officer pinned him against the cold concrete while the other violated him. They left without consequence. No arrest was made. No investigation was opened. By the time Rami found the courage to report it, three weeks had passed, and the department's response was perfunctory and ultimately dismissive.

That was twelve years ago. For the first several years, Rami had managed. He worked from home most days as a senior engineer at a mid-sized tech firm, a career that had always suited his temperament—the logic, the problem-solving, the relative solitude. But over the past decade, the assault had metastasized into something that now consumed most of his waking consciousness. He had come to believe that what happened was his fault, that something in how he had carried himself, how he had moved through that garage, had invited the violence. If he had left five minutes later, if he had taken the elevator instead of the stairs, if he had worn different clothes. The logic was circular and inescapable. What frightened him most was not that it might happen again, but that he would never recover from the knowledge that it had happened at all, that some essential capacity for joy or peace had been permanently extinguished.

The triggers were everywhere now, though some were worse than others. Sirens made his chest seize. An ambulance passing on the street sent him into a state of hypervigilance that could last for hours. He would find himself scanning the windows of his apartment, checking locks, listening for footsteps. Being alone in a room with another man—even a colleague at a rare in-person meeting, even a delivery driver—produced a suffocating dread. The presence of uniforms, the sight of a police officer, the image of a gun on a television screen: all of it sent him back to that garage, to the smell of concrete and his own helplessness.

His avoidance had become the architecture of his life. He no longer drove past his apartment building; he took a circuitous route home from the grocery store. He had not worn short sleeves in public since the assault. He refused all in-person meetings at work, a stance that had begun to strain his professional relationships. His manager had started making comments about his "commitment to collaboration." Six months ago, when the company announced a mandatory office return policy, Rami had simply stopped going in, claiming illness, knowing even as he did so that he was sabotaging himself. Last month, he had been placed on performance improvement plan. The injustice of it—that he was being punished for the aftermath of a crime no one had held anyone accountable for—had only deepened his conviction that the world was fundamentally rigged against him.

He lived now in a carefully curated safe space: his apartment, a small radius around a grocery store three blocks away, his therapist's office. Everything outside that perimeter felt dangerous. He had not seen his sister in eighteen months, had not attended his nephew's graduation. His few friendships had withered from neglect. The isolation felt necessary, a rational response to a world that had proven itself capable of casual cruelty and indifference.

It was his sister who finally insisted he seek help. She had called to say she was getting married and she needed him there, not as an obligation but because she loved him and she could not bear to watch him disappear any longer. That conversation had broken something open in him—not hope, exactly, but a recognition that the cost of his safety had become unbearable. He was fifty-four years old and he was living like a prisoner in his own home, and no amount of vigilance had ever brought him the safety he was seeking. Last week, he called a trauma therapist. He had taken the first step into her office with his hands shaking, terrified of what might happen, terrified of what might not.
